name: Selling commodity volatility (variance risk premium)

origin.source_title: Variance Risk Premia in Energy Commodities (Journal of Derivatives, 2010)

how_it_works.simple: People who buy protection against big oil price swings usually pay more than the swings turn out to cost. Sell them that protection and keep the difference, as long as no huge swing comes.
how_it_works.analogy: Like selling storm insurance: most years you keep the premiums, and one bad storm can take years of them.
how_it_works.precise: Short a 30-day variance swap on crude oil each month: payoff = implied variance at entry minus realised variance over the month. Trolle and Schwartz find annualised Sharpe ratios of 0.59 (crude) and 0.35 (natural gas) for 1996 to 2006; Prokopczuk et al. find negative payoffs for variance buyers in 18 of 21 commodity markets. With free data, OVX squared approximates the variance swap rate and realised variance comes from WTI futures.

rule: Monthly: short variance at (OVX/100)^2; realised variance from daily log returns of the rolled WTI future over the next month; size to a fixed notional; no trading costs available, so results are upper bounds.
economic_rationale: Investors pay to hedge price jumps; dealers who sell protection demand a premium.
why_it_might_fail: Short-volatility positions lose most in crises (2008, March and April 2020); variance swap and option strip costs are large and not in free data; OVX is an index, not a tradable price.

reported_results.source: Trolle and Schwartz (2010), working paper, short variance swaps
reported_results.notes: Natural gas 0.35, S&P 500 1.02 over the same period. Variance swap returns are positively skewed for the buyer, so negatively skewed for the seller.

reported_results.source: Prokopczuk, Symeonidis and Wese Simen (2017), accepted manuscript, Table 1
reported_results.notes: Long variance swap payoff negative in 18 of 21 markets, for example -8.985% on average in natural gas; payoffs more negative after 2000.

post_publication_evidence: Prokopczuk et al. (2017) extend the evidence to 21 markets and find it holds, more strongly after 2000.

relevance.reason: A direct test of the volatility idea with free data, but only as an upper bound because costs are missing.

research.notes: Added from RES-0011 and RES-0012 on 2026-10-21. Registered on 2026-10-21 as REG-0008 (oil_variance_short), not yet run.
